title: India's Most Ambitious Trade Deal Goes Live on July 15. If You Work in the UK, Read This.
excerpt: The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement eliminates tariffs on 99 per cent of Indian exports, exempts 75,000 Indian professionals from British social security payments, and aims to double bilateral trade to $120 billion by 2030.
body:
In less than three weeks, a trade agreement that took more than three years to negotiate will come into force — and for the hundreds of thousands of Indians living and working in Britain, the fine print matters more than the headline numbers.

The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA, enters into force on July 15. It is the most comprehensive free trade deal India has ever implemented, and New Delhi is deploying 1,000 advisory personnel across the country to ensure businesses are ready on day one.

## What Changes on July 15

The numbers are significant. Tariffs will be eliminated on 99 per cent of Indian export tariff lines to the UK, covering sectors from textiles and engineering goods to chemicals, pharmaceuticals, marine products and processed food. Bilateral trade, currently at approximately $56 billion, is targeted to reach $120 billion by 2030.

For British consumers, the deal means cheaper Indian imports — clothes, footwear and food products will face lower duties. For Indian exporters, particularly those in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, it opens a direct path into one of the world's most valuable consumer markets without the tariff penalty that competitors still face.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, who spent June 25 to 27 in London finalising implementation details with his UK counterpart Peter Kyle, described it as an agreement that goes "far beyond traditional trade" — encompassing technology, sovereign AI, critical minerals, defence and clean energy.

## The Social Security Clause That Could Save You Lakhs

For Indian professionals on temporary assignment in the UK, the most consequential provision may not be about tariffs at all. Under the Double Contribution Convention, which takes effect alongside the CETA, Indian workers sent to Britain by their employers will be exempt from UK social security contributions — known as National Insurance — for up to five years.

Instead of paying into both the Indian and British systems simultaneously, eligible professionals will contribute only to their home country's provident fund. Government estimates suggest this could save an average IT professional ₹30 to ₹40 lakh over a three-year stint.

The provision is expected to benefit approximately 75,000 Indian professionals and more than 900 Indian companies currently operating in the UK. An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of Indian workers sent to Britain by Indian firms will qualify.

The exemption period has been extended from the originally signed 36 months to 60 months — a longstanding demand during trade negotiations. The arrangement is reciprocal: British workers employed by UK companies in India will receive equivalent treatment.

It is important to note what the exemption does not cover. It applies only to employees on temporary assignments sent by India-based employers — not to all Indian workers in the UK. Those who benefit will still need to pay the NHS health surcharge and will not be eligible for UK social security benefits.

## Whisky, Cars and the Political Optics

The tariff cuts run in both directions. India will reduce duties on Scotch whisky from 150 per cent to 75 per cent immediately, sliding to 40 per cent over the next decade. Automotive tariffs will fall from 100 per cent to 10 per cent under a quota system. Cosmetics tariffs of up to 22 per cent will be eliminated either from day one or within ten years.

For the UK, Business and Trade Secretary Peter Kyle framed the deal as giving British exporters "an edge over international competitors," noting that India has never implemented a trade agreement of this scale — meaning the UK has an immediate first-mover advantage.

## Why NRIs in the UK Should Pay Attention

Beyond the macro numbers, the CETA reshapes everyday economics for the Indian diaspora in Britain. The UK has committed to streamlined entry for Indian professionals — including business visitors, contractual service suppliers and independent professionals — without imposing numerical restrictions or economic needs tests.

Regional partnerships are also being formalised. Birmingham-Gujarat and Manchester-Maharashtra have been highlighted as examples of sub-national corridors that the agreement is designed to strengthen, creating investment channels that connect specific Indian states with specific British cities.

At the 10th Annual UK-India Week in London, Goyal noted that the Indian delegation was the largest and most geographically diverse to visit the UK — including companies from smaller cities and first-time exporters. "India today offers a stable business environment built on trust, talent and inclusive economic growth," he said.

The message to the diaspora is clear: the agreement is not just about governments reducing tariff lines. It is about creating a framework in which Indian professionals, businesses and families in Britain operate on fundamentally different economic terms than they did before July 15.
